title: Cain and Abel
description: First two sons of Adam and Eve
wiki_lead:
In the biblical Book of Genesis, Cain and Abel are the first two sons of Adam and Eve. Cain, the firstborn, was a farmer, and his brother Abel was a shepherd. The brothers made sacrifices, each from his own fields, to God. God had regard for Abel's offering, but had no regard for Cain's. Cain killed Abel, and upon God's enquiry, responded with "Am I my brother's keeper?". God judged it murder, cursing Cain and sentencing him to a life of transience, but gave him the Mark of Cain to protect him so that he is not killed by others. Cain then dwelt in the land of Nod (נוֹד, 'wandering'), where he built a city and fathered the line of descendants beginning with Enoch. Thus, Cain was the first person born, and Abel the first to die.
Cain is interpreted in Jewish, Muslim, and Christian tradition as the first murderer and liar, and Abel the first victim. Cain and Abel have become enduring cultural symbols of fratricide and sibling conflict, referenced and reinterpreted across art, literature, theater, music, and film from medieval times to modern popular culture.

In the biblical Book of Genesis, Cain and Abel are the first two sons of Adam and Eve. Cain, the firstborn, was a farmer, and his brother Abel was a shepherd. The brothers made sacrifices, each from his own fields, to God. God had regard for Abel's offering, but had no regard for Cain's. Cain killed Abel, and upon God's enquiry, responded with "Am I my brother's keeper?". God judged it murder, cursing Cain and sentencing him to a life of transience, but gave him the Mark of Cain to protect him so that he is not killed by others. Cain then dwelt in the land of Nod (נוֹד, 'wandering'), where he built a city and fathered the line of descendants beginning with Enoch. Thus, Cain was the first person born, and Abel the first to die.
Cain is interpreted in Jewish, Muslim, and Christian tradition as the first murderer and liar, and Abel the first victim. Cain and Abel have become enduring cultural symbols of fratricide and sibling conflict, referenced and reinterpreted across art, literature, theater, music, and film from medieval times to modern popular culture.


Genesis narrative

The story of Cain's murder of Abel and its consequences is told in Genesis 4:1–18:

Now the man knew his wife Eve, and she conceived and bore Cain, saying, "I have produced a man with the help of the Lord." Next she bore his brother Abel. Now Abel was a keeper of sheep, and Cain a tiller of the ground.  In the course of time Cain brought to the Lord an offering of the fruit of the ground, and Abel for his part brought of the firstlings of his flock, their fat portions. And the Lord had regard for Abel and his offering, but for Cain and his offering he had no regard. So Cain was very angry, and his countenance fell. The Lord said to Cain, 

Cain said to his brother Abel, "Let us go out to the field."  And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel, and killed him.
Then the Lord said to Cain, "Where is your brother Abel?" He said, "I do not know; am I my brother's keeper?" And the Lord said, "What have you done? Listen; your brother's blood is crying out to me from the ground! And now you are cursed from the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand. When you till the ground, it will no longer yield to you its strength; you will be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth." Cain said to the Lord, "My punishment is greater than I can bear! Today you have driven me away from the soil, and I shall be hidden from your face; I shall be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth, and anyone who meets me may kill me."  Then the Lord said to him, "Not so! Whoever kills Cain will suffer a sevenfold vengeance." And the Lord put a mark on Cain, so that no one who came upon him would kill him.

Then Cain went away from the presence of the Lord, and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden. Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch; and he built a city, and named it Enoch after his son Enoch.


Translation notes


Origins


Etymology
"Cain" and "Abel" are English renderings of the Hebrew names. Eve's words at Cain's birth (Genesis 4:1) pun on the verb קָנָה (qānâ, "to acquire" or "to get") and the name קַיִן (qayin, "Cain"). Robert Alter and Victor Hamilton both hold that the name itself means "smith" (as in blacksmith), as in Aramaic and Arabic, also attested by Cain's descendant Tubal-cain, described as the first metalworker in Genesis 4:22. However, apart from the assonance, further links between the verb and the name is unlikely, since Hebrew names are often associated with words that sound alike regardless of meaning.
The text does not explain "Abel", as it does "Cain". McKeown suggests this is because the meaning would have been transparent to the original audience. The root הֶבֶל (hebel) means "breath", "vapour", or the air that remains after you exhale and is the word translated "vanity" or "nothing" in the refrain of Ecclesiastes; McKeown, Alter and Waltke connect it with the brevity of Abel's life. Minority interpretations include that the name is independent of the root, or that the Akkadian (Old Assyrian dialect) ablu ("son") is a more likely etymology.


Context of the story
Abel, the first murder victim, is sometimes seen as the first martyr, while Cain, the first murderer, is sometimes seen as an ancestor of evil. Some scholars suggest the pericope may have been based on the Sumerian myth Enlil Chooses the Farmer-God, in which the shepherd-god Emesh and the farmer-god Enten bring their dispute over which of them is better to the chief god Enlil, who rules in favor of Enten (the farmer). 
Some scholars view the stories of Adam and Eve and Cain and Abel to be about the development of civilization during the age of agriculture; not the beginnings of man, but when people first learned agriculture, replacing the ways of the hunter-gatherer. It has also been seen as a depiction of nomadic conflict, the struggle for land and resources (and divine favour) between nomadic herders and sedentary farmers. However, Hamilton argues that such readings do not fit the narrative because conflicts of the ancient world set nomads of the steppe against urban agricultural societies which kept their own livestock, and in this narrative the farmer Cain is driven into nomadism and ends as the founder of the first city. John H. Walton argues that the occupations are not the source of conflict; they explain the choice of offerings. He points out it is God's response to the offerings that causes the conflict. Walton compares the Sumerian tale of Dumuzi and Enkimdu, in which a shepherd god and a farmer god compete for the favour of the goddess Inanna. McKeown agrees with Walton's comparison and adds that such tensions are only background to a story concerned with acceptance by God. Walton notes brotherly conflict is a rare motif in ancient Near Eastern literature. The Tale of Two Brothers (Egyptian) is the most well-known example. However, since its conflict is over a wife, Walton concludes that the surviving literature of the region offers no close parallels to Cain and Abel.
The academic theologian Joseph Blenkinsopp holds that Cain and Abel are symbolic rather than real. Like almost all of the persons, places and stories in the primeval history (the first eleven chapters of Genesis), they are mentioned nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible, a fact that for some scholars suggests that the history is a late composition attached to Genesis to serve as an introduction. The date is also disputed: the history may be as late as the Hellenistic period (first decades of the 4th century BCE) or as early as the 9th-8th centuries BCE, but the high level of Babylonian myth behind its stories has led others to date it to the Babylonian exile (6th century BCE).

Sisters/wives

Some early commentators have speculated that Cain and Abel had sisters, usually twin sisters, although this is not attested in the text. According to Rabbi Joshua ben Karha as quoted in Genesis Rabbah, "Only two entered the bed, and seven left it: Cain and his twin sister, Abel and his two twin sisters."


Jewish tradition

In Jewish tradition, has Cain become the archetypal sinner, the first murderer, and "their instructor in wicked practices", both greedy and violent (Josephus), and archetypal egoist and a leader of others into sin (Philo). In the Testament of Benjamin Cain suffers a plague every hundred years, and those who are like him in hatred of a brother are promised the same judgment. Ancient interpreters interpreted the narrative as a conflict between good and evil: Abel was a righteous martyr, and Cain became a symbol of evil. Pirke De-Rabbi Eliezer makes him the ancestor of all the generations of the wicked.
In the Book of Enoch (22:7) from the Ethiopian Jewish canon, the soul of Abel is described as having been appointed as the chief of martyrs, crying for vengeance, for the destruction of the seed of Cain. A similar view is later shown in the Testament of Abraham (A:13 / B:11), where Abel has been raised to the position as the judge of the souls.
The Hebrew text of Genesis 4:8 says that Cain spoke to Abel but does not report what he said. Ancient translators filled the gap, in the Septuagint and the Samaritan Pentateuch with the words "Let us go to the field".. All the Targums (except Onkelos) add an expansion in which the murder follows an argument about the justice of God. In Neofiti, Cain complains that because God rejected his offering and accepted Abel's, the world is not governed justly. Abel replies that his offering was accepted because his deeds were righteous. In Pseudo-Jonathan and Neofiti the Cain also declares "There is no Judgment, there is no Judge, there is no other world", and Abel affirms each of these in turn. This debate between Cain and Abel serves to explain why God preferred Abel's offering and also why Cain killed him; Abel's blunt reference to his own better deeds could have provoked Cain's rage. It presents Cain as a denier of divine justice, a forerunner of later philosophical deniers. Cain becomes the first heretic whose wickedness rests on doubt about divine justice and future judgment, and Abel a martyr for correct doctrine. Scholars are not certain of the exact date of the addition, but many think it is from the first century AD.

Other rabbinic sources do not focus on the theological debate, but propose more worldly motives. Genesis Rabbah 22:7 proposes a quarrel over dividing the world's land and movable goods, over where the Temple should be built, or over the first Eve or a twin sister born with Abel. Pirke De-Rabbi Eliezer 21 says that Cain desired Abel's twin sister. A tosefta to the Palestinian Targum found in the Cairo Genizah mentions the justice debate as well as a dispute over dividing the flocks and the land, but says the real cause a grudge over each other's wives. The Midrash and the Conflict of Adam and Eve with Satan, posit that the motive involved a desire for the most beautiful woman. According to Midrashic tradition, Cain and Abel each had twin sisters; each was to marry the other's. The Midrash states that Abel's promised wife, Aclima, was more beautiful than Awan, Cain's promised wife. And so, after Cain would not consent to this arrangement, Adam suggested seeking God's blessing by means of a sacrifice. Whoever God blessed would marry Aclima. When God openly rejected Cain's sacrifice, Cain slew his brother in a fit of jealousy and anger. Rabbinical exegetes have discussed whether Cain's incestuous relationship with his sister was in violation of halakha.
The Mishnah uses Genesis 4:10, ("blood(s) cries out from the ground") in Sanhedrin 4:5 to warn witnesses in capital cases that destroying one life is like destroying a whole world, interpreting it as Abel's blood and that of his descendants who would have been born to him. It also records a second explanation, that Abel's blood was spattered over trees and stones. Targum Neofiti speaks of "the righteous multitudes that were to arise from Abel".


Christian tradition


Matthew and Luke
In Matthew 23:35 (paralleled in Luke 11:51), Jesus uses Abel as the archetype of the righteous martyr in his polemic against the Pharisees, when talking about them killing the prophets:

"...so that upon you may come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar." 
John Nolland notes that this representation could be either chronological (the first righteous martyr to the latest one), or canonical. Matthew also uses the imagery of "the ground" on which the blood is spilt in Genesis 4:10. 


Hebrews
Hebrews 11:4, makes a brief reference to the Cain and Abel story:

grok_lead: Cain and Abel, the first two sons of Adam and Eve as depicted in the Book of Genesis in the Hebrew Bible, represent the inaugural narrative of human conflict and fraternal rivalry following the expulsion from Eden. Cain, the elder son, becomes a farmer who works the soil, while Abel tends flocks as a shepherd; both brothers bring offerings to God, but only Abel'sâdescribed as the fat portions from the firstborn of his flockâis regarded with favor, provoking Cain's anger and jealousy. Their story unfolds through acts of sacrifice, divine preference, jealousy, murder, and subsequent divine judgment, encapsulating themes of moral choice, the consequences of sin, and the establishment of human societal norms. In a field, Cain rises against Abel and kills him, marking the Bible's first recorded murder and introducing themes of sin, divine judgment, and human rebellion. When confronted by God, Cain denies knowledge of Abel's whereabouts, prompting a curse that dooms him to a fugitive and wanderer existence, as the ground he once tilled will no longer yield its strength. Fearing retribution, Cain expresses despair over his punishment's severity, leading God to place a protective mark on him to deter vengeance from others, with a promise of sevenfold retribution against any who harm him. Subsequently, Cain departs from the presence of God and settles in the land of Nod, east of Eden, where he builds a city and fathers descendants, including Enoch. The story of Cain and Abel has profoundly influenced theological, ethical, and cultural interpretations across Abrahamic traditions, symbolizing the tension between agricultural and pastoral lifestyles, the dynamics of divine acceptance versus rejection, and the persistence of violence despite warnings against sin "crouching at the door." Scholars highlight its exploration of sibling rivalry, shame, and the origins of human moral failing, positioning it as a foundational narrative for understanding fratricide and exile in Judeo-Christian tradition. Eve later bears Seth as a replacement for Abel, underscoring themes of loss and continuity in the human lineage.
